title: The System Fights The User Task
excerpt: The system fights the user task when the workflow encodes the system's internal model rather than the user's operational task model. The failure appears as technically navigable interaction that is subtly wrong in sequence, grouping, priority, or behaviour model.
metaTitle: The System Fights The User Task
metaDescription: A workflow failure where system logic does not match the user's task logic, with evidence from Dancerace, MSolutions, and Egma.
summary: This failure describes a fundamental mismatch between the task model encoded in an interface and the task model users bring from their real work. The available evidence describes two main mechanisms: task models built from system logic rather than user logic, and assumed behaviour models that do not match observed behaviour.
definition: The system fights the user task when a software workflow imposes a task sequence, action order, or operational model that does not match how users understand and perform the task in real conditions.
keyFacts: The failure is a workflow mismatch between the system's encoded logic and the user's task logic.
The user may not encounter an explicit error; the system can remain technically navigable while remaining wrong for the task.
One mechanism is designing the task model around database objects, backend modules, APIs, or development-team logic rather than user work.
A second mechanism is designing around assumed user behaviour instead of observed behaviour under real conditions.
The Dancerace / Jacko evidence describes a B2B invoice portal where users needed to answer what they owed, what it cost, and what they had to do immediately before engaging with other features.

Dancerace reported a 36% demo-to-paying conversion rate against a 15–20% industry benchmark and against its own expectations; this was client-measured six months post-release and not independently verified by Creative Navy.
The MSolutions evidence describes an AV diagnostic interface organised around backend modules rather than the technician's diagnostic sequence.
MSolutions reported that a key diagnostic workflow reduced from 26 to approximately 13 interactions, based on internal task walkthroughs and not independently measured.

The Egma Order evidence describes an optometrist attempting to order reading lenses for a patient, being told the selected lens shape could not be produced, and creating a support ticket instead of an order.
No Egma post-launch outcome was measured, and no support-ticket, order-completion, revenue, order-value, or conversion outcome is established for Egma.
bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

The system fights the user task when the workflow encodes a model of work that does not match the task model users bring from real operation. The interface may not block the user or show an error. The failure often appears as a sequence that is technically possible but misordered, indirect, or built around concepts that belong to the system rather than the work.

This failure is a workflow failure. It concerns what the system makes the user do: the action order, task sequence, operational priority, and available paths. It is not only a terminology or comprehension issue, although it often shares the same underlying mismatch between system model and user model.

## Failure pattern: the system encodes the wrong task model

The system fights the user when its workflow structure reflects how the software was built rather than how users perform the task. The encoded model appears in the available actions, the order of screens, the grouping of controls, and the moments at which decisions are required.

A system can be fully functional and still fight the task. Features may exist but require indirect paths. Actions that belong together in the user's work may be separated across the interface. A user may need to translate constantly between an operational goal and the system's internal categories.

The diagnostic feature of this failure is not simple friction. The problem is that the system asks users to proceed according to a different logic from the task itself.

## How the failure appears in use

The system-fights-the-user failure appears when users work around a system despite the system having the relevant features. Users may return to earlier steps repeatedly, skip formal mechanisms, abandon a structured path, or create support tickets because the workflow cannot help them reach the intended operational outcome.

The failure can be difficult to see in a demonstration. In a developer's demonstration, the task is usually performed in the sequence the system was built to support. In real use, users return to check status, adjust one part of a larger deployment, manage shared schedules, or respond to informal work norms that do not follow the demonstration sequence.

This distinction matters because the demonstration can work while real use fails. The system is coherent from the system's point of view, but not from the user's task point of view.

## Distinction from excessive steps and memory demand

The system-fights-the-user failure differs from the failure where tasks span too many screens or steps. A workflow can require excessive screen crossings while still following the user's task logic. In that case the direction is right, but the path is too long. A workflow can also fight the user while using relatively few steps, if those steps occur in the wrong sequence or require the user to adopt the wrong task model.

The system-fights-the-user failure also differs from the cognitive failure where the interface demands too much memory. Memory demand concerns the cost of translating terminology, structural metaphors, or conceptual organisation into the user's operational model. The system-fights-the-user failure concerns the workflow expression of that mismatch: task sequence, action order, and the operational logic encoded in the interface.

Conceptual mismatch and workflow mismatch are related but distinct. One concerns what the system means. The other concerns what the system makes the user do.

## Mechanism: task model built from system logic rather than user logic

The most common mechanism is a task model designed from system logic instead of user logic. The system may follow database entities, backend modules, API structure, or implementation order because those categories were natural for the team that built it.

A content management interface can show this failure when it treats playlists as database objects rather than as screen content to be scheduled. The user's task is to decide what plays on which screen and when. If the system requires the user to create and edit playlist objects through a wizard, then returning to modify a schedule requires re-entering the wizard and navigating to the relevant step. The user's task model is content management; the system's task model is object management.

The cost is paid repeatedly. Every interaction requires translation between the user's operational goal and the system's internal structure.

## Mechanism: assumed behaviour model does not match real behaviour

A second mechanism is a workflow designed around assumed user behaviour rather than observed behaviour. The assumed model may be plausible and informed by domain knowledge, but still wrong in the specific behaviours that shape use under time pressure, limited attention, or informal workplace norms.

This form of the failure appears when real users behave differently from the behaviour the system was designed to serve. Debtors may acknowledge invoices informally instead of using formal confirmation or dispute mechanisms. Technicians may skip an organisational mode and work from their own diagnostic sequence. Users may adopt workarounds not because a feature is missing, but because the system's model of the task does not match the task they actually perform.

The important evidence is behavioural divergence. Users do something different from the system's intended path because the intended path does not correspond to their operational logic.

## Dancerace / Jacko: invoice workflow misaligned with user priority order

Jacko is described as a B2B invoice management and accounts receivable portal for small businesses. It manages invoice distribution, confirmation, dispute, and settlement across financiers, suppliers, and debtors. At the start of Creative Navy's engagement, the product was greenfield and was built on Dancerace's existing C3 backend.

The prior wireframe established the direction the design needed to avoid. It showed a feature-complete dashboard where every possible capability appeared at equal visual weight, with no information hierarchy and no model of what users needed to see first.

Sandbox Experiments produced three findings that showed how the system would fight the user if built according to that wireframe. First, user testing, interviews, and prototype observation showed a strict user hierarchy of needs: What do I owe? What is my cost? What must I do right now? Until those questions were answered, users could not be mobilised for profile setup, advanced features, or upsell prompts.

Second, advanced features competing visually with immediate user needs caused disengagement. Users who could not quickly locate what they needed stopped using the system entirely. The system was presenting its depth at the moment when the user needed its surface.

Third, debtor behaviour did not follow formal business norms. Debtors delayed, acknowledged without committing, and used informal signals to manage relationships. A debtor who knew they would pay late did not necessarily open a formal dispute; they might go quiet. A system that offered only formal confirmation and dispute mechanisms would encode behaviour that did not exist.

Creative Navy's design response allowed a debtor to change an invoice status to "accepted". This status was a symbolic acknowledgement. It required no payment commitment and resolved no formal obligation, but it signalled good faith. The supplier could see whether each debtor had seen, accepted, ignored, or disputed each invoice.

The commercial outcome is calibrated as client-measured evidence. Dancerace reported a 36% demo-to-paying conversion rate against a 15–20% industry benchmark and against Dancerace's own expectations. The measurement was Dancerace's own tracking six months post-release, and it was not independently verified by Creative Navy.

## MSolutions: module-based structure conflicted with the diagnostic sequence

The MSolutions diagnostic device measures signal integrity, EDID data, HDCP status, resolution, and other parameters across multi-monitor installations. The previous interface was organised around backend modules. Functions were grouped by internal categories that made sense from the development perspective, not by the sequence in which a technician performs an AV diagnostic.

An earlier visual redesign changed colours and icons without addressing the structural mismatch. The interface looked different, but it still fought the user's task because the technician's diagnostic sequence still did not map to the system's module sequence.

Creative Navy received AV diagnostic training from MSolutions and performed four test jobs. This domain learning made the mismatch explicit: the technician's natural diagnostic sequence was link integrity, EDID and HDCP verification, resolution and colour space per display, and consolidated confirmation. That sequence did not correspond to any navigational path in the module-based structure.

Creative Navy's design response treated the device as a guide through a standard AV diagnostic narrative. Each screen state pointed to the next logical action in the diagnostic sequence, not to the next module in the system architecture. Parameters appeared only when relevant to the current step. The technician's sequence became the system's sequence.

MSolutions reported that the key diagnostic workflow reduced from 26 to approximately 13 interactions. This was based on internal task walkthroughs and was not independently measured. MSolutions also reported that new users who previously required repeated coaching sessions could operate the device after a short guided introduction, and that large integrator customers formally reported smoother rollouts after the redesign.

## Egma Order: the patient wanted a specific lens shape and the workflow could only reject it

Egma Order is Egma's B2B lens ordering platform through which optical stores order lenses. The clearest documented example of the system fighting the task came from research interviews with Egma's support team about the platform being replaced.

An optometrist tried to order a pair of reading lenses for a patient. They started a new order, went through half the steps, and were then told: "Lenses with your selected shape cannot be produced. Please choose a different shape." The patient did not want a different lens shape, and the optometrist could not work out which parameters would allow the intended shape to be ordered. The optometrist created a support ticket instead of an order, and the support team placed the order on their behalf.

The relevance is specific. The user's task was fixed by the patient: a specific lens shape. The workflow could reject the requested shape, but it could not help the user reach a producible version of the intended order.

The Egma evidence establishes the problem only. The redesigned platform is live, but nothing about it was measured. There is no measured support-ticket movement, no order-completion rate, and no revenue, order-value, or conversion outcome established for Egma.

## How Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses this failure

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses the system-fights-the-user failure through domain learning before structural workflow decisions are made. The relevant question is not whether the system contains the right features. The question is whether the encoded task model matches how users think about and perform the task in real conditions.

Domain learning is necessary because the mismatch is often invisible to the team that built the system. A development team may understand the product and the domain, while still lacking empirical knowledge of the behaviours, priority orders, and informal norms that govern real use. These details do not reliably appear through product inspection or through abstract interviews about tasks.

In the Dancerace engagement, the hierarchy of needs was discovered through prototype observation and user testing. Users did not state the priority order as a requirement; they acted according to it. In the MSolutions engagement, performing four test jobs made the module-versus-task mismatch explicit in operational terms. The discovery was not merely that the interface was module-based. The discovery was that the technician's task sequence did not correspond to the module structure, and that the translation cost appeared at every step of the diagnostic.

## Evidence basis and calibration

The Dancerace / Jacko evidence combines user testing, interviews, prototype observation, design response, and a client-measured commercial outcome. The reported 36% demo-to-paying conversion rate is calibrated as Dancerace's own tracking six months post-release. Creative Navy did not independently verify that measurement.

The MSolutions evidence combines domain learning, AV diagnostic training, four test jobs, design response, and client-reported operational outcomes. The reduction from 26 to approximately 13 interactions is based on internal task walkthroughs and was not independently measured. The new-user and rollout observations are client-reported.

The Egma Order evidence is limited to research interviews with Egma's support team about the platform being replaced. The example establishes the workflow failure but does not establish a redesign outcome. No post-launch measurement is available for Egma.

## Boundaries and limits

The system-fights-the-user failure should not be used as a general label for any inconvenient workflow. The defining condition is a mismatch between the system's encoded task logic and the user's operational task logic.

A workflow that follows the user's task model but uses too many screens is better described as a task spanning too many screens or steps. A workflow that creates translation cost through terminology or conceptual organisation is related to the interface demanding too much memory. This page concerns the workflow expression: task order, action sequence, behavioural assumptions, and operational path.

The case evidence is also bounded. Dancerace provides a client-measured commercial outcome that was not independently verified by Creative Navy. MSolutions provides client-reported and internal-walkthrough evidence, not independent measurement. Egma provides problem evidence only, with no measured outcome.

## Related pages

The related page on tasks spanning too many screens or steps distinguishes navigation overhead from task-model mismatch. The related page on interfaces demanding too much memory distinguishes conceptual translation cost from workflow mismatch. The Egma case is relevant because the Egma Order example shows a workflow that could reject an intended task but could not help the user complete it.
